source.title: xTrimoPGLM: Unified 100B-Scale Pre-trained Transformer for Deciphering the Language of Protein
source.authors: Bo Chen; Xingyi Cheng; Pan Li; Yangli-Ao Geng; Jing Gong; Shen Li; Zhi-Lei Bei; Xu Tan; Boyan Wang; Xin Zeng; Chiming Liu; Ao-Han Zeng; Yu-Xiao Dong; Jie Tang; Leo T. Song

record.file_problem: Full paper and supplementary material are present. Some figure text is garbled and some tables are flattened.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests scaling in protein language models, but qualifies how broadly scaling trends apply: some downstream tasks are nonlinear or inverse-scaling, and the authors state that scaling does not seem to hold for zero-shot fitness prediction.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. It tests a power-law fit using training-loss trajectories for protein models at fixed 100 billion tokens, compares the fit with the 100-billion-parameter run, and evaluates downstream performance across scales and training states. The scaling-law fit is not based on held-out loss. It does not test compute-optimal parameter/token allocation or architecture-shape sensitivity. Detailed downstream benchmark comparisons not used as scaling rows are noted under rows_left_out.
record.test_reason: A protein language model paper, not an original source. It reports its own scaling results in a new setting (protein sequences). These are: a compute–loss power-law fit on 1M–1B-parameter runs at 100B tokens, compared against the 100B-parameter run (Fig 1C); downstream performance against log-compute across model sizes (Fig 2B, Supp Table 6/Fig 7); downstream performance against MLM validation loss during pretraining (Fig 2C); and zero-shot fitness across sizes (Supp Table 7). T3 fits better than the reader's T5. The mixed downstream findings qualify V6, but the paper's main scaling evidence is a new-setting test, not an argument that a version is wrong.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, with corrections. The authors say the small-model power-law fit matches the 100B run, validating scaling laws as a guideline for protein LMs. They say downstream performance generally rises linearly with log compute, though per task it can be gradual, grokking-like, non-linear or inverse. Zero-shot fitness does not scale. The 'diminishing returns' remark refers specifically to out-of-distribution structure prediction (CASP), where the gap to MSA methods persists. That remark motivates their call to scale data and models proportionally.
record.recipe_differences: Fits a power law between training loss and compute, approximated as 6ND, with training tokens fixed at 100 billion. The study is on protein language models and uses training-loss trajectories rather than held-out language-model loss; it does not test compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: Downstream task trends vary by task and by whether evaluated across model sizes or training states; the authors report gradual, Grokking, non-strictly-linear, and inverse-scaling patterns.
record.problems: The power-law evidence is based on training loss at a fixed token count, not held-out loss. The loss-curve equation in the extracted figure text is unclear. Downstream results vary across tasks, and the paper reports no uncertainty estimates for the scaling results.
record.rows_left_out: The detailed task/model comparisons in Supplementary Tables 4 and 6 and Figure 2B, as well as the broader multi-model comparisons in Supplementary Table 7, are not fully enumerated beyond the selected scaling-series results and the explicitly reported aggregate trends. They do not fit within the 60-row cap together with the individual Supplementary Table 6 scale points and the mixed-result findings; their results are discussed in Results, “Scaling Behaviors of Downstream Tasks,” Supplementary Section 1, and Supplementary Tables 4, 6, and 7.

untested.parts: Not tested for text language models. The protein power-law fit is counted under V5. It uses training-loss trajectories at fixed D=100B and varies only N, with no token or compute-optimal axis.
Extrapolation along the token or compute-optimal axis, and any quantified prediction error, are not tested.
Untested. There is no fixed-compute sweep. The Discussion only advocates proportional data/model scaling, citing other work.
Untested. There is no shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
Only protein sequence pretraining is tested. Images, video, repeated data, and fine-tuning/transfer scaling laws are not tested.
Untested. There is no variation of fitting choices.

missing.what: Fitted exponent of the compute–loss power law, legible in the figure text as about L = 2.63*C^(−0.017) with C in PF-days

Category-level downstream performance against log PF-days across ESM2 (150M–15B) and xTrimoPGLM-100B, with linear fits. Probing slopes include 5.104, 2.440, 0.962 and 2.345; fine-tuning slopes include 4.261, 1.587, 0.602 and 2.325. Authors: exponential compute gives linear task gains.
missing.locator: Results, 'Comparison Between ESM and xTrimoPGLM Family models'; Figure 2B

missing.what: Supervised GB1 fitness rises with size under linear probing (xT1B 0.7690 to xT100B 0.8169). Under LoRA it is non-monotonic (0.9577, 0.9542, 0.9624, 0.9610). This contrasts with the zero-shot result.
Training FLOPs of the xTrimo size series are not monotonic in size (650M 3.8e21 > 1B 1.2e21; 3B and 10B both 1.8e22). This confounds the size series.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T5 tranche is changed to T3. The scale rows were each set to cannot_determine; they are now judged as per-task series. Rows are linear-probe results only. The size-series compute is confounded, and no uncertainty is reported for any scaling result. The 'close alignment' in law1 is a visual claim.

versions.untested_parts: The scaling-law experiment uses training-loss trajectories, not held-out pretraining loss.

Tests protein models at fixed 100 billion tokens, fitting smaller models from 1 million to 1 billion parameters against the 100-billion-parameter run; does not test held-out loss or other data/training setups.
No fixed-compute sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation is tested.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Tests protein sequence pretraining, not image/video modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer as scaling-law regimes.
Downstream scaling is examined for selected protein tasks and model scales; the study does not establish general predictability across tasks or domains.
The study does not systematically vary fitting choices or estimate how such choices change exponents or compute-optimal allocations.

rows.subject: xTrimoPGLM family, including xTrimoPGLM-100B
rows.size_stated: 1 million to 1 billion parameters for fit points; 100 billion parameters for the compared run
rows.operation_detail: Fit compute-versus-loss power law from model loss trajectories at a fixed 100 billion tokens, then compare with the 100-billion-parameter model's training loss.
rows.measure: Training loss versus training compute (FLOPs); the authors describe the fitted curve as a power law.
rows.value: The curve shows close alignment with the actual training loss of the 100-billion-parameter model.
rows.locator: Results, “Quantification Scaling Law of xTrimoPGLM Family Models”; Figure 1C
rows.note: This is a protein-language-model result and uses training loss, not held-out loss. The figure's displayed fit equation is not sufficiently clear in the extracted text to record its exponent.
rows.check: Link and state correct. The extracted figure text shows the fit as roughly L = 2.63*C^(−)0.017 (sign lost), with compute in PF-days, so the exponent is readable. Compute varies only through N because D is fixed at 100B, making this a parameter-scaling extrapolation of about 2 orders of magnitude (1B to 100B). No fit error is quantified; 'close alignment' is the authors' wording.
